items.item: events routed through a retry path are not guaranteed to be processed in the same sequence received in the source topic, because the retry path is slower and has fewer instances

Retrying a poison record in place isn't a smaller version of this problem — it's a structurally different failure, because the ordering guarantee that makes the retry safe to attempt is the exact mechanism that also blocks everything behind it.

Diverting a record off the partition doesn't fix the underlying failure — it only relocates where that failure's cost is paid, from availability (a stalled partition) to consistency (broken relative order).

A tiered retry schedule is a bet about failure duration, not failure cause — it buys a record time to recover from a transient fault, but offers nothing against a fault that is permanent from the first attempt.

A dead-letter record's value is entirely in what it carries, not in the fact that it exists — a record dead-lettered with no original offset or exception is no more actionable than one silently dropped.

The ordering cost this topic names isn't unique to retry topics — it's the same at-least-once-style trade this chapter has made before (duplicates traded for availability), applied here to sequence instead of delivery count.

Kafka Connect's errors.tolerance and Kafka Streams' DLQ handler solve the same problem at different layers of the same ecosystem, which is why Streams needed its own mechanism even after Connect already had one.

A retry topic and a dead-letter topic are the same primitive — a separate topic holding records the main flow can't currently handle — used at two different points of a record's life: mid-retry versus retry-exhausted.

The toy BlockingPartition and NonBlockingRetryFlow models are deliberately simplified standalone demonstrations, not ports of a real Kafka cluster's retry machinery, and the orders processed in each run are this run's own output, not cited figures.

Deduplication and dead-lettering solve opposite failure directions: dedup assumes a record can eventually succeed and guards against seeing it twice; dead-lettering assumes a record can never succeed and guards against it blocking everything else.

Naming the ordering cost explicitly, rather than leaving it implicit, is what lets a downstream consumer decide whether strict order actually matters for its own logic — an undisclosed cost can't be designed around.

A dead-letter topic being bounded and observable is what makes it fundamentally different from an infinite retry loop or a silent drop — both of those also 'handle' exhaustion, just without leaving anything an operator can act on.
